items.title: Anthropic's amended S-1 reports $16.96B Q3 revenue — roughly 1.7x OpenAI's reported $10B Q3, with the Nov 18-19 pricing book reportedly 'multiple times oversubscribed' at $70-$78 and up to 20% carved out for retail investors
items.summary: Anthropic's amended S-1 filing (S-1/A), dated November 10, 2026, reports approximately $16.96 billion in revenue for the quarter ended September 30, 2026 (Q3) — up roughly 47% quarter-over-quarter from Q2 — and a Q3 operating loss of about $567 million. The same filing sets the proposed IPO range at $70 to $78 per share across 825 million shares (with other filings describing 801.4M new Class A shares plus 23.6M secondary), implying a top-of-range raise around $64 billion and a valuation in the broad neighborhood of $1.0 trillion to $1.4 trillion, depending on the valuation method used (reporting varies: ABC News cites ~$1.3 trillion; other outlets cite ranges between ~$1.0 trillion and ~$1.5 trillion). Anthropic will trade as 'ANT' on the Nasdaq Global Select Market, with pricing set for Wednesday, November 18 and trading expected to begin Thursday, November 19. A special Class F share held through an entity controlled by Anthropic's seven co-founders represents 50.1% of overall shareholder voting power, preserving founder control post-IPO. The Q3 figure sits alongside a reported (but not filed) OpenAI Q3 revenue of approximately $10 billion, surfaced by The Information and relayed through FirstSquawk and Yahoo Finance; OpenAI is private and does not file revenue with the SEC, so this is secondary reporting rather than a filed number. The direct comparison is imperfect in one important way: Anthropic's S-1/A states that it recognizes cloud-marketplace revenue on a gross basis, which inflates headline revenue relative to a net-of-reseller-cut accounting method; CNBC's coverage flags that Anthropic and OpenAI account for cloud-marketplace sales differently. On an apples-to-apples basis, the gap would narrow, though direction of advantage likely still holds. Four further signals from the filing and surrounding coverage have sharpened the picture over the last 24 hours. First, Bloomberg reported on November 11 that the order book is 'multiple times oversubscribed' at the $70-$78 range, with large anchor-size orders driving the demand; a secondary FourWeekMBA headline cites a '$115B+ book, 1.3x SpaceX' figure, but the underlying reporting does not give a dollar size, so treat the $115B number as unverified. Second, Anthropic has reportedly reserved up to 20% of its Class A shares for retail investors — JPMorgan is leading the US retail distribution and Citigroup is coordinating international retail — a share that is high for a tech IPO at this scale. Third, AI Weekly reports that Nvidia and Google will each take approximately $10 billion of the offering as anchor investors, and that bankers are now weighing whether to price the deal at a $1.5 trillion+ valuation rather than the midpoint of the filed range. A separate Reuters-sourced report mentions a parallel $26 billion private placement alongside the public float. Fourth, Anthropic hosted a live-streamed conversation between CEO Dario Amodei and JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon on Friday, November 13 — an unusual roadshow move explicitly designed to draw retail participation; no transcript or recap has surfaced as of this writing. Commentary citing the filing also surfaces approximately $895 billion in multi-year compute commitments and roughly 900% net revenue retention (SaaStr) — both of which, if accurate, are the primary explanations for the Q3 revenue jump: dollar-expansion from the existing enterprise base rather than net-new-logo growth.
items.why_it_matters: This is one of the quieter big stories of the week because the data point lands in a filing rather than through a product launch — and over the last 36 hours the roadshow signals have moved the story from 'will they price' to 'how far above the range.' Four threads worth noticing. First, this is the first public-filing data point where a frontier-lab revenue leaderboard has flipped. Anthropic has been the smaller-revenue lab in nearly every public comparison for three years — behind OpenAI on consumer usage, behind OpenAI on total revenue. A filed $16.96 billion Q3 against OpenAI's reported $10 billion Q3 is the first filing-grade reading that puts Anthropic ahead. The structural explanation appears to be enterprise contract concentration: the roughly 900% net revenue retention figure cited by SaaStr implies very high dollar-expansion within an established enterprise customer base, and Claude Code specifically has been earning higher per-seat ARR than ChatGPT consumer subscriptions since mid-2026. The counter-signal is the accounting-basis caveat: on a net-of-cloud-reseller-cut basis, the comparison is likely tighter than 1.7x, and OpenAI probably still leads on consumer-facing monetization when ChatGPT Plus and Pro subscriptions are included. Read both numbers as directionally correct but not literal head-to-head totals. Second, the $567 million Q3 operating loss is the sleeper detail. If accurate, Anthropic is losing roughly 3.3% on each revenue dollar at Q3 scale. OpenAI's Q1 operating margin was reported at approximately negative 122%, and Q2 was reportedly worse — the structural gap in unit economics between the two labs is probably the single most important fact in frontier AI right now. It means Anthropic can plausibly raise capital at IPO-grade valuations with a visible path to self-funding, while OpenAI's capital needs keep scaling with revenue growth. For Gabe, this matters because it is the first filing-grade evidence that frontier labs can run as real businesses at $10 billion-plus quarterly scale, not as growth-fueled science projects. The Claude Code pricing structure ($20 Pro, $100 Max, $200 Max+) that Anthropic has been quietly stable on all year is probably the unit-economics story — and it is the pricing book worth paying attention to for anyone who wants a sustainable AI-coding subscription over the next 12 months. Third, the 'multiple times oversubscribed' signal is the one that moved the gross-vs-net accounting question off center stage. When the book is covered multiple times at the $70-$78 range, bankers generally price at or above the top of the range regardless of methodology debates. The anchor positions — reportedly ~$10B each from Nvidia and Google — are the market signal that matters: both companies have their own frontier-model programs (Nvidia through strategic investments, Google through Gemini) and are putting capital behind a direct competitor at IPO prices. Nvidia's position is especially notable given the ongoing Jensen Huang succession story; a $10B commitment one week into a CEO transition is either a strong vote of confidence from the board/Kress or a pre-committed order that cannot easily be unwound. Fourth, the 20% retail carve-out and the Amodei-Dimon livestream on November 13 are the structurally interesting detail for the next 12-24 months of AI-company IPOs. Reserving a fifth of the deal for retail — plus marketing it through a live-streamed CEO conversation — is the Robinhood-era playbook, not the traditional institutional-roadshow playbook. For any US-based individual with a brokerage account who wants direct exposure to Anthropic rather than through Amazon's or Google's holdings, this is the most accessible route they will get. Expect every subsequent frontier-lab IPO (OpenAI, xAI eventually) to study the Anthropic retail-allocation structure as the reference design. The pricing window to watch is Wednesday November 18 after the close, with trading Thursday November 19; a price above $78, or a trading pop materially above the offer price, cements the gross-basis accounting method as the new default for frontier-AI valuation conversations.

items.title: Fireworks AI's October breach widens to customer secrets, datasets, and incomplete model weights — Notion disconnects, disables Insights; Cursor and Harvey also named; cloud provider still unidentified 5 days on
items.summary: On November 9, 2026, inference platform Fireworks AI expanded the disclosure of its second October security incident. In the updated bulletin, the company said an unauthorized party reached stored secrets, datasets, and incomplete model weights for a limited set of accounts, along with customer billing and account data more broadly. The access path was a compromise of an unnamed third-party cloud provider hosting Fireworks' R&D machines on October 23, with an unauthorized workload running on Fireworks development machines on October 24. This is distinct from an earlier October incident — first disclosed on roughly October 6 and investigated by Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 — in which an unauthorized party used internal Fireworks credentials to reach environment variables holding API keys and tokens for a limited number of customer accounts. Fireworks has attributed the new activity to an actor it believes is linked to the financially-motivated 'LLMJacking' trend — stealing inference credentials to run paid workloads on the victim's account. Payment card numbers were not exposed; Fireworks does not store them. Three named customers are working with Fireworks on impact assessment: Notion, Cursor, and legal-AI company Harvey. Notion's own advisory (vendor notice November 2 or November 6 depending on source; Notion-side action timestamps November 3) says fewer than 1% of its workspaces may have been affected — specifically unattributable Notion AI chat sessions used for its Insights feature. Notion has disabled Insights, disconnected from Fireworks (November 3), deleted its data at Fireworks, stopped all data and traffic, halted all training runs, and stopped serving open-weight models through Fireworks. Workspace owners can review affected data through an in-product security-incident review page available on desktop and web (not mobile), accessible only to workspaces with managed members. Harvey says none of its data was affected. Cursor-specific impact has not been publicly confirmed. Fireworks has also disabled self-service dataset uploads and downloads used by Batch Inference and dataset-based training while the investigation continues. Its Inference service, Training SDK, and Nexus — which keep no customer data by default — appear not to have been impacted, though the investigation is ongoing. Fireworks CEO Lin Qiao has fronted the customer-notification correspondence in subsequent coverage. Five days after the expanded disclosure, the identity of the third-party cloud provider remains undisclosed, as do the exact number of affected files or customers and the mechanism by which the internal credentials used in the first incident were obtained. Reporting also mentions that some large-spend customers are reportedly considering alternative providers, though the sourcing is anonymous.
items.why_it_matters: This matters for anyone who builds on hosted AI infrastructure, which now effectively means anyone writing agents on top of a model API. Three practical threads. First, the supply-chain-blast-radius is the real lesson. A single compromised cloud host at Fireworks has now reached billing data, secrets, datasets, and incomplete model weights at a vendor whose named customer list includes Notion (writing and knowledge work), Cursor (developer coding), and Harvey (legal). That is three different verticals downstream of one upstream failure. The pattern — a shared inference platform becoming the single point of compromise for downstream apps that assume they are serving their own users — is the thing to internalize. Any Python agent calling a hosted model endpoint sits inside a similar dependency graph, and the mitigation is the same regardless of which inference provider is in the hot seat this week: rotate keys at any inference vendor you have ever sent data to, keep a second provider warm, and assume logs are sometimes retained even when zero-retention is the headline marketing claim. The ongoing silence on the cloud-provider identity — five days after the expanded disclosure — is itself a signal: Fireworks either does not want to name a hyperscaler partner (which would make the provider's own customers nervous), or there is active legal negotiation about attribution. Either way, the practical read for a developer is 'assume your inference vendor's upstream dependencies are opaque' — not a new fact, but the first week where it has cost named customers production features. Second, Notion's response is a useful reference design worth studying. Within days of the vendor notice, Notion disabled the affected feature (Insights), terminated the vendor connection, deleted its data at the vendor, stopped all training runs through the vendor, stopped serving open-weight models through the vendor, and surfaced the incident to workspace owners through an in-product review page. That is a clean chain of actions, and the separation between the user-facing feature and the vendor relationship is the architectural choice that made the fast cutover possible. If you are designing a product that sends user data to a hosted model, build it so the vendor can be swapped or turned off at the feature level — not only as a whole-product migration — and keep a plain-English description of what data each vendor sees. Third, the 'LLMJacking' framing is the piece worth knowing about by name. The attacker profile Fireworks describes is not a nation-state or an espionage operator; it is a financially-motivated group stealing inference credentials to resell compute or run paid workloads on the victim's account. For a hobbyist with a $20/month ChatGPT or Claude subscription that is background noise. For anyone with a corporate OpenAI/Anthropic/Together/Fireworks key stored in a .env file, a GitHub Actions secret, or a shared config, LLMJacking is now the realistic threat model — more likely than targeted data exfiltration. The practical steps: rotate the key, scope it narrowly (project-level rather than account-level where providers allow), enable per-key spend limits, and watch for unexpected usage spikes. Notion's bulletin also mentions rotating any secrets that may have ended up inside an AI chat with the platform, which is a good reminder that chat logs with AI assistants are secret-material by default and should be treated that way.
items.why_it_matters_brief: Five days on, the compromised cloud provider is still unnamed — the supply-chain opacity is the real lesson for anyone storing inference keys in a .env file, and LLMJacking is now the realistic threat model.

items.title: Anthropic launches Claude Meetings in beta for Google Meet — joins calls as a visible participant and can draft plans and timelines live; also ships Claude Whiteboards, Sheets beta, and moves Claude Data to GA
items.summary: On November 10, 2026, Anthropic launched Claude Meetings in beta for Team and Enterprise plan users, with Google Meet as the first supported platform. Claude joins the call as a visible participant and can answer questions during the meeting, draft plans and timelines on a Claude Whiteboard in real time, and generate follow-up materials. The same announcement introduced Claude Whiteboards and Claude Sheets (both in beta on paid plans) and moved Claude Data — previously called Claude Dashboards — to general availability. Support for other video conferencing platforms is planned but no dates were given.
items.why_it_matters: Anthropic is building out Claude beyond the chat interface at a steady clip. Claude Meetings is the most visible sign of that — moving from 'AI you consult after a meeting' to 'AI that participates in the meeting itself.' Whether that's useful depends heavily on the team's work patterns, but the access level is higher than a notetaker: Claude is reading the conversation live and can respond mid-meeting. The companion launches matter at least as much as the headline: Claude Whiteboards (live collaborative whiteboard during the meeting), Claude Sheets (AI-native spreadsheets in beta), and Claude Data (formerly Dashboards, now GA) round out what looks like a deliberate push into workspace-productivity territory. For Gabe, the most practical near-term relevance is Claude Sheets in beta — an AI-native spreadsheet that can interact with live data is the kind of tool worth watching as it moves toward GA. The enterprise gating (Team + Enterprise only at launch) is a signal that Anthropic is prioritizing high-ARR business usage, consistent with the 900% NRR story in the IPO filing. The Google Meet partnership first (not Zoom or Teams) is likely tied to the Google Workspace partnership track rather than a neutral platform choice.
items.why_it_matters_brief: Anthropic moved Claude from chat into live meetings — it joins Google Meet calls as a visible participant, can draft plans and timelines live, and ships Claude Sheets beta and Claude Data GA alongside it.

items.title: Moonshot AI (Kimi) confidentially files for Hong Kong IPO at ~$50B valuation — first major Chinese frontier-AI lab to pursue a public listing as Kimi K3 drives ARR to $300M
items.summary: Moonshot AI, the Beijing-based lab behind the Kimi assistant and Kimi K3 reasoning model, has confidentially filed for an initial public offering on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange, with a reported target raise of between $3 billion and $5 billion and an indicative pre-IPO valuation of approximately $50 billion. The valuation marks a rapid jump from the company's $35 billion close on a $3.5 billion funding round in mid-2026, and from roughly $4.3 billion in late 2025. Moonshot's ARR reportedly reached $300 million by June 2026, up from $200 million in April, driven primarily by the Kimi K3 reasoning model. Keling AI, a video-generation spinout, has also reportedly filed separately. No listing date has been confirmed; some estimates put the first quarter of 2027 as the likely window.
items.why_it_matters: Moonshot AI going public would be the first IPO from a major Chinese frontier-AI lab, and it is happening almost simultaneously with Anthropic's US listing — a data point on how the AI-lab investment cycle is playing out in both hemispheres at once. The valuation path (from roughly $4B at end-2025 to $50B now) reflects the broader pattern of Chinese AI labs scaling fast on domestic demand: Kimi competes with Alibaba's Qianwen and Baidu's Ernie for Chinese-market users, and Kimi K3's strong reasoning benchmark performance has earned it real usage share. For context, Moonshot's $50B target is roughly 3% of Anthropic's $1.4T filed valuation — a significant gap, but Moonshot is also a much younger company and operating in a tighter regulatory environment for outbound capital. The Keling AI simultaneous filing is worth watching separately: AI video generation is a fast-moving segment and a standalone public listing would give it a market price independent of the LLM narrative. The broader takeaway is that the first cohort of Chinese frontier-AI lab IPOs is arriving, and the Hong Kong exchange is the primary venue — which matters for understanding how the global AI-capital cycle will look in 2027.
items.why_it_matters_brief: Moonshot AI is the first major Chinese frontier-AI lab to pursue a public listing — the $50B valuation is 10× in one year, and the HK IPO timing mirrors Anthropic's US listing almost exactly.
